title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Philadelphia, PA: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Philadelphia shipyard, refinery and bridge welders: code book choice, Part B planning, eligibility. Online or at your site.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Preparation in Philadelphia: Six Days for Shipyard, Process and Bridge Welding Inspectors
html:
Philadelphia welds ships at the old Navy Yard, keeps a ring of process plants running along the Delaware, and rebuilds highway and transit steel that carries a large share of the Northeast Corridor's traffic. The people who check that work, whether they sit in a shipyard QA office, a fabricator's quality department or a testing agency's truck, are increasingly asked to hold the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) credential. Atlantis NDT's six-day CWI exam-preparation course is built for the welders, fitters, QC inspectors, NDT technicians and engineers in this region who intend to take that exam.

The American Welding Society writes the CWI exam; AWS administers it, scores it and issues the certificate. Atlantis stands outside that process. Its job is preparation; it issues no certification, sees no exam content, and has no approval or endorsement from AWS. Eligibility, the vision test and the exam itself are between you and AWS. What Atlantis supplies is structured preparation: online study with an instructor answering questions for people working alone, or the full six days taught at an employer's own premises for a group. The national six-day CWI course page sets out every day in detail.

A city that welds ships, process pipe and bridges at once

Few metros pack three distinct welding economies into such a small footprint. Within a short drive of Center City you can find a commercial shipyard, the remains and the survivors of a large refining complex, and a steady program of bridge and highway rehabilitation. Each one uses a different code family and a different idea of who the inspector works for, which is why the code book choice for Part C deserves more thought here than it would in a single-industry town.

The sections below take each economy in turn, then cover the local AWS section, where welders train, how the exam logistics work from Philadelphia, and how the six days fit a candidate or an employer in the Delaware Valley.

The Navy Yard: commercial shipbuilding and what it asks of inspectors

The shipyard at the former Philadelphia Naval Shipyard is the city's most visible welding employer. Hanwha completed its purchase of Philly Shipyard at the end of 2024, and the yard now operates as Hanwha Philly Shipyard. It has built commercial vessels for the domestic trade and, in recent years, the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel training ships for the U.S. Maritime Administration.

Shipbuilding puts unusual weight on a few parts of the CWI body of knowledge. Panel lines and block assembly use a lot of submerged arc and flux cored welding, so process knowledge and the discontinuities each process produces matter. Fit-up on large plate assemblies makes misalignment, root opening and distortion daily topics. Hull and deck work is built to classification society rules and the owner's specification rather than to AWS D1.1 alone, so a shipyard inspector must be comfortable moving between documents. Where Navy or federal work is involved, NAVSEA technical publications set their own inspector qualification rules, and the yard qualifies its people under them. A CWI is respected background in that setting but is not a substitute for those requirements.

For a shipyard QC technician, the six-day course tends to fill gaps in metallurgy and code navigation rather than in shop knowledge. Most yard workers can spot porosity or undercut by eye; fewer can find the right acceptance table in a code book quickly under exam conditions.

After the refinery: South Philadelphia and the Delaware Valley process belt

For more than a century, South Philadelphia hosted the largest refining complex on the East Coast. The Philadelphia Energy Solutions refinery shut down after the explosion and fire of June 2019, and the site has since been sold for redevelopment. That closure removed a large source of maintenance welding from the city itself, but it did not end process work in the region.

Refineries still operate at Trainer in Delaware County, at Paulsboro across the river in New Jersey, and at Delaware City downstate. Marcus Hook, once a refinery town, is now a natural gas liquids hub fed by the Mariner East pipelines across Pennsylvania. Chemical plants, tank terminals and utility stations fill the gaps between them. All of that equipment needs repair welds, alterations and periodic replacement during planned shutdowns, and that work runs on ASME Section IX for welding qualification, ASME B31.3 for process piping and the owner's own specifications. API RP 577 is the reference many owner inspectors use for welding inspection and metallurgy in refinery settings.

Contractors who work in this belt often need a CWI on the crew to verify fit-up, preheat, interpass temperature and weld profile before the owner's API inspector or engineer reviews the package. Atlantis supports owners in the region through refining NDT consulting for the Philadelphia area and sends technicians for piping inspection and weld inspection in Philadelphia.

Infrastructure: I-95, the Delaware River crossings and transit steel

In June 2023 a tanker truck fire beneath Interstate 95 in Northeast Philadelphia brought down an elevated section of the highway. The emergency rebuild that followed reminded the region how much of its traffic rides on steel and concrete structures maintained by PennDOT and its contractors. Day to day, that maintenance is less dramatic but constant: bearing replacements, steel repairs, deck and joint work on interstates and city viaducts.

The four major Delaware River bridges operated by the Delaware River Port Authority (the Ben Franklin, Walt Whitman, Commodore Barry and Betsy Ross) are large steel structures with long-running rehabilitation programs. SEPTA's rail, trolley and elevated lines add stations, viaducts and maintenance facilities. Steel bridge fabrication and repair follow AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, under state and owner specifications, and the fabricators and erectors who do it need welding inspectors who understand fracture-critical members, cover plate terminations and the extra scrutiny bridge work receives.

On building projects, the Philadelphia Building Code, administered by the Department of Licenses and Inspections, is based on the International Building Code and its special inspection provisions, which bring third-party welding inspectors onto steel-framed buildings. Those inspectors usually work to AWS D1.1 for the structure, with the design documents setting the acceptance criteria.

Who signs for welds in Philadelphia, and what each employer wants

  • Shipyard quality departments look for inspectors who handle process-heavy production work and can read class and owner specifications as easily as AWS codes.
  • Structural and bridge fabricators in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware need in-house QC inspectors; for bridge work, D1.5 fluency is the differentiator, and AWS offers a D1.5 endorsement.
  • Testing and special inspection agencies send inspectors to building sites under the city's code and to transit projects. They want a D1.1 CWI who writes clear daily reports.
  • Construction inspection consultants working for PennDOT and other owners hire welding inspectors for bridge and highway contracts.
  • Mechanical contractors in the process belt want CWIs who know ASME Section IX and B31.3 and can keep up with turnaround pace.
  • NDT and inspection companies sell visual weld inspection alongside UT, MT and PT, so a candidate who brings a CWI plus employer-certified NDT skills is easier to put on a job.

The question to ask before you start studying is which of these employers you want to sign for. The answer usually decides your Part C code book.

The AWS Philadelphia Section

AWS divides its members into districts and local sections. The Philadelphia Section belongs to AWS District 2. Section meetings, plant tours, student competitions and scholarship events bring together working CWIs, welding engineers, educators and students, and they are worth attending while you prepare. Experienced inspectors at those meetings can tell you which code book local employers expect, how they organized their experience records, and which parts of the practical took them longest. Officer contacts and meeting venues change, so use the District 2 listing on aws.org for current details.

Community College of Philadelphia and the naval welding pipeline

The Community College of Philadelphia runs a Welding Technology program that trains structural, pipe and specialty welders with a clear eye on shipbuilding and defense work. The college describes the curriculum as aligned with NAVSEA technical publications and MIL-STD workmanship standards, with preparation for AWS D1.1 performance qualification testing. It lists AWS Certified Welding Inspectors among its instructors, alongside NAVSEA-qualified instructors, and it names BlueForge Alliance, a defense workforce organization, as a source of placement support. Training takes place at the college's Career and Advanced Technology Center.

A welder coming out of that kind of program has a good base for Part A. Symbols, joint geometry and process knowledge will be familiar, and exposure to inspection-readiness topics helps with the practical. What remains is time: AWS requires welding-related work experience before you can sit the CWI exam, so most graduates spend several years on the shop floor or the waterfront before the course becomes relevant. The guide to CWI requirements and career impact explains the timing.

Getting to each part of the exam from Philadelphia

The three parts of the CWI exam are delivered in two different ways. Fundamentals (Part A, 150 questions) and Code Application (Part C, open book, roughly 50 to 65 questions) both run on a computer in a Prometric test center. AWS reports more than 100 of those across the United States, and a Philadelphia candidate will usually find one within reach. You schedule them with the eligibility code from the AWS confirmation letter.

The Practical (Part B) is different. It is hands-on work with AWS-supplied tools and specimens plus 46 related questions, and it runs at AWS seminar locations on dates tied to the seminar schedule. Look up the closest location and its next dates on aws.org before you commit to a study plan; the Part B date often sets the whole timeline. AWS requires a minimum of 72% on each part.

AWS sets and publishes its own exam and seminar fees on aws.org. To estimate the full outlay, including code books and time away from work, the planning calculator for CWI exam spending is a useful start.

Picking a Part C code book in the Delaware Valley

Part C allows one book on the desk. Among the choices AWS accepts are the Bridge Welding Code D1.5, the structural steel code D1.1 in its 2020 edition, the pipeline standard API 1104 in its 22nd edition, and an ASME option pairing Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3. Editions change, so check aws.org before you order anything.

Background reading: the structural steel code overview, the pipeline welding standard summary and the explainer on WPS, PQR and welder qualification records. Atlantis does not write or qualify welding procedures, but every CWI candidate has to read them.

The six days, seen from a Philadelphia shop floor

The course runs the same six blocks for every candidate. What changes from city to city is which examples make the material stick.

  • Day 1, Fundamentals I: processes, joint design, AWS A3.0 vocabulary and AWS A2.4 welding symbols. Shipyard candidates often find the submerged arc and tandem process material easy and the symbol drills harder.
  • Day 2, Fundamentals II: how steel responds to heat, what tensile, bend and impact tests prove, why flaws form, which NDT method finds which flaw, shop safety, and the inspector's obligations. Refinery contractors usually want more time on preheat, postweld heat treatment and hardness.
  • Day 3, Practical: reading gauges correctly, checking leg size and contour, and judging welds against a supplied set of specifications. A group taught on its own premises works with the company's gauges and shop samples, because Atlantis does not send replica kits.
  • Day 4, Code application: working inside your chosen book, from clause layout and tables to acceptance criteria and qualification limits.
  • Day 5, Timed practice: practice papers for Parts A, B and C against the clock, then a full review of every miss.
  • Day 6, Review and exam readiness: weak areas, pacing, and a checklist for the AWS application and its supporting documents.

Atlantis writes its own practice items from the topic list AWS publishes, and not one of them is lifted from an AWS paper. A candidate preparing alone works online on their own schedule and messages the instructor with questions. An employer such as a fabricator in Bucks County or a contractor in Delaware County can have the six days taught at its own facility for its staff. The course sets out what will be covered; it makes no promise about exam results.

Experience and eligibility for shipyard and refinery workers

AWS sets the experience you need against your education, and the full table is on the national page. In plain terms: a high school graduate needs five years of welding-related work, a candidate with completed trade or vocational welding courses needs four, and an associate degree in engineering technology, engineering or physical science brings it down to two. Shorter schooling raises the requirement to nine or twelve years.

Shipyard workers sometimes split time between welding, fitting and other trades; only the welding-related portion counts, and AWS decides what qualifies. Turnaround contractors often have many short jobs with different employers, which makes verification harder, so keep a running list of dates, employers, codes and supervisors. Eyesight is checked separately on the AWS visual acuity record, and the examination date needs to fall inside the window AWS allows after that eye test.

Once you hold the card: renewal, endorsements and NDT

AWS says a CWI lasts nine years, with renewal applications in the third and sixth years and a recertification step at the ninth, where the listed routes include a Part B retake, 80 professional development hours or Certified Radiographic Interpreter status. Endorsements that suit Philadelphia work include D1.5 bridge welding, API 1104 pipeline, ASME Section IX, and the magnetic particle and penetrant testing endorsements. The Senior CWI pathway article covers the next rung.

Many CWIs go on to perform NDT as well. NDT certification under ASNT SNT-TC-1A comes from the employer, against its written practice, and Atlantis trains people toward it: see VT Level 1 training, NDT Level 2 training and the full list of NDT training options for Philadelphia. The side-by-side of CWI, API 577 and ASNT Level II explains how the three differ.

Candidates elsewhere in the Northeast can compare the Baltimore CWI prep page, the New York page and the Pittsburgh page.

Request a quote for Philadelphia candidates

Tell Atlantis how many people are preparing, which code book each plans to use, whether you want online access for individuals or the six days at your site, and where that site is. Use the Philadelphia CWI exam prep quote form. Atlantis replies within one business day.

faq.q: Which code book suits a Philadelphia shipyard worker?
faq.a: Hull and deck work is built to class and owner rules, so no single AWS book covers it. Many shipyard candidates take AWS D1.1 for Part C because its structure, acceptance tables and qualification clauses carry over well, then rely on yard training for class requirements.

faq.q: I do refinery and chemical plant maintenance. What should I use for Part C?
faq.a: The ASME option, built on Section IX together with B31.1 and B31.3, matches the documents used across the Delaware Valley process belt. Confirm the current option and editions on aws.org before buying books.

faq.q: Where is the CWI exam taken near Philadelphia?
faq.a: Fundamentals and Code Application are computer tests at Prometric centers, booked with the eligibility code AWS sends you. The Practical is held only at AWS seminar locations on scheduled dates, so check aws.org for the closest one.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a training center in Philadelphia?
faq.a: No. Individual candidates prepare online and can put questions to an instructor; employers in the region can have the six days taught at their own plant, yard or shop. Atlantis offices are in Houston and Hyderabad.

faq.q: Is a CWI enough for Navy work at a shipyard?
faq.a: Not by itself. Navy and NAVSEA-governed work has its own inspector qualification rules, and the yard qualifies its people under them. The CWI remains valuable for commercial, structural and code work around the region.

faq.q: Can bridge inspectors use the course?
faq.a: Yes. The six days follow the CWI body of knowledge, and candidates working on PennDOT or river-crossing steel can choose AWS D1.5 or D1.1 for Part C and practise inside that book on Day 4.

faq.q: Do the practice papers contain real AWS questions?
faq.a: No. Atlantis drafts each item itself from the subjects AWS lists for each part, so nothing on a practice paper comes out of a real examination.

faq.q: What NDT training can I add after the CWI?
faq.a: Atlantis runs training built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A; certification then comes from the company you work for, under its own written practice. Start with NDT training for Philadelphia.

faq.q: How do I ask for a Philadelphia quote?
faq.a: Send candidate numbers, code books and your site location through the Philadelphia CWI quote form. Atlantis replies within one business day.
